title: The alveolar meshwork of nucleus and cytoplasm is a surface-tension froth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The alveolar meshwork of nucleus and cytoplasm is a surface-tension froth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The alveolar 'reticulum' seen in the nucleus and cytoplasm is a froth or foam produced by the interacting surface tensions of two intermixed fluids of similar density striving to separate, and is not inherent in the nature of protoplasm.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: This phenomenon is nothing else than what we call in ordinary language, a “froth” or a “foam.” It is a surface-tension phenomenon, due to the interacting surface-tensions of two intermixed fluids, not very different in density, as they strive to separate.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Alveolar meshwork as a froth”. Scope: nuclear and cytoplasmic alveolar meshworks of cells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Foam topology and response to tension are distinct from membrane and cytoskeletal alternatives. Existing imaging can reject broad versions, but exact identification of Thompson's alveoli and matched physical measurements limit complete resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare live and fixed-cell images of alleged alveolar networks and test whether their geometry and dynamics match two-fluid foam predictions and vary with interfacial-tension perturbations. Persistence as membrane- or cytoskeleton-defined structures with incompatible topology would refute the foam mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Interfacial tensions are usually not measured alongside images.

The historical structure may not map uniquely to a modern organelle.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Foam geometry is a quantitative signature, and public live versus fixed images can ask whether the reticulum is present in living cytoplasm. That tests the main factual content for well-imaged cell types. It does not directly show two fluids striving to separate, so a network that is real but cytoskeletal would refute the foam account only where junction angles and continuity are measured.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In living and unfixed cells, test whether the alveolar meshwork has foam geometry, including threefold junctions near 120 degrees, as expected for two immiscible fluids, and whether that meshwork is absent when fixation is avoided. Foam geometry in living cells would support the claim; a meshwork that appears only after coagulation, or a living network with filament geometry, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical fixatives are only partly matched by modern correlative datasets.

Interfacial tension of the supposed fluids is not in the image metadata.

Cytoskeletal networks can mimic a mesh without being a two-fluid foam.

data existence: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.55
